content: The hydroperoxyl radical (HO2), also known as the perhydroxyl radical, is the protonated form of superoxide. The equilibrium between protonated and deprotonated forms is governed by a pKa of approximately 4.8. This means that in the cytosol of a typical cell, about 0.3% of the superoxide present exists in its protonated form, HO2. Despite this, the scientific literature disproportionately focuses on superoxide, with only 28 articles mentioning HO2, hydroperoxyl, or perhydroxyl in their titles, compared to 9,228 articles discussing superoxide. This discrepancy is argued to be unjustified, as the biological and biomedical significance of HO2 is likely much greater than the attention it has received. Recent findings suggest that many biological and chemical phenomena can be more effectively explained by considering the involvement of HO2. A broader recognition of the potential roles of HO2 in biological systems could significantly advance biomedical research. The pKa of HO2 is highly influenced by the dielectric constant of its environment. In the atmosphere, where the dielectric constant is very low, superoxide generated photochemically is almost entirely present as HO2. Due to its high reactivity, HO2 plays a critical role in atmospheric chemistry by breaking down certain organic pollutants, effectively acting as a cleanser of the atmosphere. This makes the chemistry of HO2 highly relevant to geochemical processes. The standard enthalpy of formation and standard entropy values for HO2 at 298 K were provided by Martin J. Rabinowitz from NASA Lewis Research Center.
